citation: Dubovi, I., Levy, S. T., & Dagan, E. (2017). Now I know how! The learning process of medication administration among nursing students with non-immersive desktop virtual reality simulation. Computers & Education, 113, 16-27. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.05.009
thesis: A non-immersive, desktop-VR simulation (PILL-VR) produces significantly greater and better-retained conceptual/procedural learning of a clinical skill (medication administration) than matched lecture-based instruction, and generates presence scores matching or exceeding published immersive-VR norms; the authors argue presence is induced by representational fidelity and interactive control rather than by immersive hardware, extending Witmer & Singer's (1998) own unconfirmed presence-increases-learning hypothesis.

sections.title: Introduction (1-1.4)
sections.summary: Frames the theory-practice gap in nursing education around medication-administration training; introduces PILL-VR (OpenSim desktop VR); reviews non-immersive vs. immersive VR and Witmer & Singer's (1998) four presence factors (control, realism, distraction, sensory input); surveys inconsistent meta-analytic evidence on non-immersive VR in health-care education (Cook, Erwin & Triola 2010 vs. Consorti et al. 2012); states two research questions on learning gains and on the presence/performance mechanism.

sections.title: Methods (2.1-2.5)
sections.summary: Quasi-experimental pretest-intervention-posttest comparison-group design, non-randomized (diffusion-avoidance rationale); experimental group n=82/104 completers trained 3 hours with PILL-VR, comparison group n=47/73 completers (prior academic year) received an equivalent-duration lecture; describes the PILL-VR hospital-ward architecture, nurse-avatar, 45-minute acclimation phase, and two graded scenarios; describes the MAP knowledge questionnaire, the Hebrew-validated Presence Questionnaire, and worksheets/screen-video coding for n=10.

sections.title: Results (3.1-3.2)
sections.summary: PILL-VR group shows significantly higher learning gains than comparison group on overall MAP score and all subscales (largest for Administration Sequence), retained to a five-month delayed post-test; video/worksheet coding shows a declarative/procedural dissociation and an in-VR error-reduction effect from scenario A to B; Presence Questionnaire scores match or exceed Witmer & Singer's (1998) immersive-VR norms; small significant positive correlation between the Involved/Control presence subscale and MAP learning scores.

sections.title: Discussion (4-4.2)
sections.summary: Interprets results via Fitts & Posner's (1967)/Anderson's (1983, 2009) three-stage skill-acquisition model and dual-channel/multimedia-learning theory (Baddeley et al. 2009; Clark & Paivio 1991; Mayer 2014); reframes presence as fidelity/control-induced rather than immersion-induced (citing Lee, Wong & Fung 2010); states limitations (non-randomization, dropout, an instrument asymmetry between groups, small video subsample); concludes VR simulation functions as a safe, low-cost 'deliberate practice' mechanism transferring declarative to procedural knowledge.

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: PQ subscale scores (Involved/Control 5.2±0.7; Natural 4.7±1.03; Interface Quality 5.0±1.1) match or exceed Witmer & Singer's (1998) own immersive-VR norms despite non-immersive hardware

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: operationalized as the Involved/Control PQ subscale; framed as the presence factor most proximate to learning; the 45-minute free-exploration acclimation phase is the mechanism by which control is built before graded scenarios

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs. germane)
constructs.treatment: PILL-VR's multisensory (visual+auditory) cueing argued to reduce extraneous cognitive load per dual-channel theory and Mayer's (2014) signaling/cueing principle, supporting the cognitive stage of skill acquisition

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: MAP questionnaire's Medication Administration Sequence subscale shows the largest gain; video coding reveals a declarative/procedural dissociation on first attempt, resolving by the second scenario

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: learning gains held from two-month post-test to five-month delayed post-test (repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni post hoc non-significant post-vs-delayed, p=.14)

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: named directly, alongside interactive control, as the source of presence, displacing immersion/hardware as the operative variable

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: thinly present — students enter as a nurse-avatar and explore their 'avatar-body' during acclimation; not theorized beyond descriptive mention

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR (PILL-VR)
conditions.design: quasi-experimental pretest-intervention-posttest, non-randomized, comparison group drawn from prior academic year to reduce diffusion
conditions.instruments: MAP knowledge questionnaire (13 items, 3 subscales, alpha=0.78); Witmer & Singer (1998) Presence Questionnaire, Hebrew-validated (Kizony 2006, alpha=0.89; this study alpha=0.88), 3 subscales; worksheets + Camtasia screen-video for n=10 subsample
conditions.effectDirection: significantly higher learning gains than comparison group on overall MAP and all subscales; retained at 5 months; PQ scores match/exceed immersive-VR norms; small positive presence-learning correlation (r=.211-.231)

conditions.label: conventional instruction (control)
conditions.design: lecture-based curriculum, two pharmacists, PowerPoint, 3-4 hours
conditions.instruments: MAP knowledge questionnaire (pre/post only; missing Reasoning & Accountability subscale at pre-test)

conditions.label: screen-based virtual patient / sim
conditions.design: P/anticipatory-application — the authors never use this label, but PILL-VR's nurse-avatar interacting with an animated patient in a scripted clinical scenario structurally resembles the virtual-patient condition this cluster's Strand-D column tracks (cf. ped-sec-19 Kononowicz)

readings.claim: PILL-VR produced significantly higher conceptual/procedural learning gains than lecture-based instruction on the overall MAP score and every subscale, largest for Administration Sequence.
Learning gains were retained without significant decline from the two-month post-test to a five-month delayed post-test.

Declarative and procedural knowledge dissociate within the VR environment: near-complete worksheet declarative knowledge co-occurred with frequent first-attempt in-VR procedural errors, read as valuable 'error recovery' feedback.
A non-immersive desktop system produced presence scores matching or exceeding Witmer & Singer's (1998) immersive-VR benchmarks.
Presence is induced by representational fidelity and interactive control, not by immersive hardware per se.
The small positive correlation between the Involved/Control presence subscale and learning offers a design principle: ensuring sufficient user control is an important condition for learning.

interlocutors.name: Witmer, Bob & Michael Singer
interlocutors.role: source of the Presence Questionnaire and its four presence factors; source of the unconfirmed presence-increases-learning hypothesis this paper extends

interlocutors.name: Fitts, Paul & Michael Posner
interlocutors.role: source of the three-stage skill-acquisition model applied to interpret PILL-VR's learning process

interlocutors.name: Mayer, Richard E.
interlocutors.role: cognitive theory of multimedia learning; signaling/cueing principle used to explain PILL-VR's multisensory cueing effect

interlocutors.name: Clark, James & Allan Paivio
interlocutors.role: dual coding theory, supporting the cognitive-load account

interlocutors.name: Baddeley, Alan, Michael Eysenck & Michael Anderson
interlocutors.role: working-memory theory, supporting the cognitive-load account

interlocutors.name: Lee, Eric, Kevin Wong & Chun Che Fung
interlocutors.role: companion desktop-VR SEM finding cited to support presence-without-immersion claim

interlocutors.name: Cook, David A., Patricia Erwin & Marc Triola
interlocutors.role: 2010 meta-analysis on computerized virtual patients, cited for inconsistent non-immersive-VR evidence in health-care education; ****** UNVERIFIED: not confirmed whether this is the same David A. Cook author series as ped-sec-15 (Cook et al. 2011 Technology-Enhanced Simulation meta-analysis) — treat as a distinct citation unless verified

interlocutors.name: Consorti, Fabrizio et al.
interlocutors.role: 2012 meta-analysis reporting a positive pooled effect of desktop VR vs. normative instruction, cited as the counter-finding to Cook, Erwin & Triola

interlocutors.name: Merchant, Zahira et al.
interlocutors.role: cites a 2014 K-12/higher-education VR-instruction meta-analysis; same lead author as this cluster's ped-sec-16 (2012 chemistry desktop-3D study) but a different paper — intra-cluster citation-network signal, not a same-paper match

interlocutors.name: Tüzün, Hakan & Filiz Özdinç
interlocutors.role: 2016 study on 3D MUVE presence and learning, cited as parallel supporting evidence for the presence-learning link

tensions.axis: presence as immersion/hardware-determined vs. presence as fidelity/control-determined
tensions.note: The paper explicitly takes the fidelity/control side against an implicit immersion-determined default, citing Lee, Wong & Fung (2010) as a companion finding; directly relevant to this cluster's debate-axis 3 (presence as technology-determined vs. psychologically/individually determined).

tensions.axis: non-immersive VR effectiveness in health-care education: negligible (Cook, Erwin & Triola 2010) vs. positive pooled effect (Consorti et al. 2012)
tensions.note: The paper positions its own strong positive result as additional evidence on the Consorti side of this unresolved meta-analytic disagreement, without directly reconciling the two prior meta-analyses.

tensions.axis: desktop-3D as a sufficient, cost-effective proxy for IVR vs. IVR's unique affordances
tensions.note: The paper's central claim (fidelity/control over immersion) supports the desktop-3D-is-sufficient pole of this cluster's debate-axis 5, though the study contains no direct IVR comparison condition and so cannot itself adjudicate the debate.
